title: The Man Whose Muscles Leaked
synopsis: Mr. Gustavo Diaz arrives in the ED with progressive proximal weakness and myalgias, his heart racing at 110 and lactate climbing. The culprit is a contraindicated drug combination — simvastatin plus gemfibrozil — that has poisoned his muscle mitochondria, spilling CK into his bloodstream and threatening his kidneys with myoglobin.

chapters.heading: Disruption
chapters.body: Mr. Gustavo Diaz walks into triage slowly, his thighs burning with each step. He grips the counter to steady himself, then eases into a chair, exhaling hard. The triage nurse takes vitals and finds his heart rate at 110, his respiratory rate at 22, and a lactate of 2.3 — his body is working harder than it should, and his muscles feel like they are tearing from the inside.
chapters.visualHint: Wide three-quarter shot of Mr. Diaz in triage, one hand on the counter, face tight with effort, gown open at the back, bare feet visible at the bottom edge of the frame.

chapters.heading: Embodiment
chapters.body: When Dr. Oppong asks him to stand from the chair, Mr. Diaz cannot push up without using both arms — his hip flexors and quadriceps have no power. He describes a deep ache in his shoulders and thighs that started three days ago, and now even lifting a coffee cup feels heavy. The weakness is proximal, symmetric, and tender to palpation.
chapters.visualHint: Medium close-up on Mr. Diaz's hands gripping his own thighs as he tries to rise, his face clenched, the doctor's hand extended but not yet touching.

chapters.heading: Escalation
chapters.body: Dr. Oppong reviews his medication list and stops cold: simvastatin 40 mg plus gemfibrozil 600 mg — a contraindicated combination. Gemfibrozil blocks the glucuronidation pathway that normally clears statins, so simvastatin levels have skyrocketed. At toxic concentrations, the drug poisons mitochondrial function in skeletal muscle, starving the cells of ATP. Without energy, the sarcolemma cannot maintain its electrochemical gradient, and the membrane fails.
chapters.visualHint: Close-up on the medication list on the chart, the two drug names highlighted by a finger, the doctor's face in soft focus behind it.

chapters.heading: Crisis point
chapters.body: The CK result comes back at 48,000 U/L — more than ten times the upper limit of normal. This is not a test of damage; it is a direct measure of membrane rupture. The higher the CK, the more cells have died. His urine is dark brown, and the dipstick is positive for blood without red cells on microscopy — myoglobinuria. His creatinine is still normal, but the myoglobin is already poised to hit his kidneys and cause pigment nephropathy.
chapters.visualHint: Medium shot of the lab slip in Dr. Oppong's hand, the CK value circled, with Mr. Diaz's dark urine bag visible in the background.

chapters.heading: Mechanism turn
chapters.body: Dr. Oppong discontinues both drugs immediately and starts aggressive IV fluids at 200 mL per hour to flush the myoglobin through the kidneys before it can precipitate in the tubules. The goal is to prevent acute kidney injury while the muscle cells stabilize. He explains to Mr. Diaz that the weakness will take days to improve, but the real danger now is renal — and fluids are the only proven protection.
chapters.visualHint: Wide shot of the ED bay: IV pole running wide open, Mr. Diaz lying back with a blanket over his legs, the nurse adjusting the drip rate.

chapters.heading: Recontextualization
chapters.body: Once the CK trends down and renal function is confirmed stable, Dr. Oppong will switch Mr. Diaz to atorvastatin or rosuvastatin — statins that are not metabolized through the glucuronidation pathway — and if a fibrate is still needed, fenofibrate instead of gemfibrozil. The episode is a lesson in drug interactions that nearly cost this man his kidneys and his ability to walk.
chapters.visualHint: Medium shot of Dr. Oppong sitting at the bedside, speaking calmly to Mr. Diaz, the monitor showing a heart rate of 88 and a normal blood pressure.
